raw_evidence.label: Genre bias in IMDb connections
raw_evidence.content: Sci-fi, horror, action and comedy films are over-represented in connection counts because they generate quotable lines, iconic shots, and parody-friendly tropes. Star Wars (4965 references) and The Wizard of Oz (3291) lead the all-time list — neither won Best Picture. Psycho's shower scene, Jaws' two-note theme, and Terminator's 'I'll be back' are referenced thousands of times. By contrast, intimate dramas that win Best Picture — Spotlight, Moonlight, The Artist, Birdman — are rarely parodied or visually quoted. The dataset captures a specific kind of cultural memory: the kind that propagates through pastiche.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: Past 'Academy got it wrong' moments
raw_evidence.content: Cinephile lore is full of cases where the Academy passed over the era-defining film: Citizen Kane lost to How Green Was My Valley (1941). Star Wars lost to Annie Hall (1977) — a fine film, but not the cultural earthquake Star Wars was. Pulp Fiction lost to Forrest Gump (1994). Goodfellas lost to Dances with Wolves (1990). Saving Private Ryan lost to Shakespeare in Love (1998). The connections data offers a way to quantify these gaps: when the eventual winner has fewer references than a non-nominated film, the Academy demonstrably failed to crown the most-influential film of its year. The benchmark question: how often does this happen, and is the rate increasing?

The Academy systematically passed over the era-defining genre films.

print("\n=== ana_06 ===")

raw_evidence.label: Biggest snubs: year-#1 vs the actual Best Picture winner
raw_evidence.content: The most extreme mismatches are striking. In 1933 King Kong got 1,053 references and Cavalcade — the actual Best Picture winner — got 8: a count_ratio of 131. In 1931 Frankenstein had 72x more references than Cimarron. Snow White had 60x The Life of Emile Zola in 1937. In the modern era, Empire Strikes Back outpaced Ordinary People 18.6x (1980), Psycho beat The Apartment 16x (1960), and Star Wars: The Force Awakens dwarfed Spotlight 11.5x (2015). These aren't quirks — they are systematic gaps where the most-referenced film of the year was not even nominated.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_16 ===")
unnom = df[(df["year_rank"] == 1) & ~df["result"].isin(["W", "N"])].copy()
# attach the BP winner of that year for comparison
winner_lookup = winners.set_index("oscars_year")[["movie_name", "count", "annual_share"]].rename(
    columns={"movie_name": "winner_name", "count": "winner_count", "annual_share": "winner_share"}
)
snubs = unnom.merge(winner_lookup, left_on="oscars_year", right_index=True, how="left")
snubs["count_ratio"] = snubs["count"] / snubs["winner_count"]
snubs = snubs.dropna(subset=["winner_name"]).sort_values("count_ratio", ascending=False)
cols = ["oscars_year", "movie_name", "count", "annual_share", "winner_name", "winner_count", "count_ratio"]
print("year-#1 (not nominated) vs that year's actual BP winner — biggest gaps:")
print(snubs[cols].head(20).to_string(index=False))

1980 Empire vs Ordinary People: 1748 vs 94, ratio=18.6

raw_evidence.content: This dataset was built by The Economist's Graphic Detail team for a story published on March 2, 2019, days before the 91st Academy Awards. The story coincided with Green Book's controversial Best Picture win, sharpening the argument that the Academy's choices increasingly diverge from cultural memory.

raw_evidence.label: What an IMDb 'movie connection' is
raw_evidence.content: IMDb's connections include any explicit reference one piece of media makes to a film: dialogue quotes ('Of all the coffee joints in all the towns in all the world...' nodding to Casablanca on Frasier), camera-technique homages, parodies (the scary strings from Psycho), poster cameos, plot spoofs, visual references, and clip insertions. They are crowdsourced — fans submit them and IMDb editors curate. The mechanism rewards films that are quotable, visually iconic, or culturally pervasive enough that audiences and creators recognize the reference. Films that won critical acclaim but produced no quotable images or moments tend to score low. This is why genre cinema (sci-fi, horror, thrillers, action) dominates the rankings while many Best Picture dramas trail.

raw_evidence.label: The recency problem
raw_evidence.content: A film from 1965 has had 50 extra years to accumulate references compared to a film from 2015. Connections counts therefore are not directly comparable across decades — they confound cultural impact with simple time elapsed. The Economist's solution was annual share: each film's count divided by the total references for all films released in the same year. Within any single year, share is a fair comparison; across years, it is still imperfect (older years are saturated and stable, the most recent years are still accruing). The chart deliberately ranks films within years rather than across years, but trends in the top-1 share or top-10 concentration over time can still be read.

raw_evidence.label: Top 20 most-referenced films of all time

Ten films in the top 20 were never even nominated, including Empire Strikes Back, Psycho, The Terminator, and 2001: A Space Odyssey.

raw_evidence.label: Best Picture: ceremony rules and Oscar year quirks
raw_evidence.content: For the first six Academy Awards (1927/28-1932/33) the eligibility window crossed calendar years (August to July). The Economist collapsed this into a single oscars_year per film. Wings, the first 'Outstanding Picture' winner, was released in 1927 but is filed under 1928 and received its award at a 1929 ceremony. Some early classics like Metropolis (1927) and Steamboat Willie (1928) appear in the data even though they were technically ineligible (foreign / animated short) — the Economist kept them as orientation anchors. From 1944 onward, exactly one Best Picture winner and four to nine nominees per year are tagged. Best Picture has been the headline award since the very first ceremony in 1929.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the Oscars' cultural authority
raw_evidence.content: The Academy Awards are the most-watched film awards in the world and have historically functioned as a canonization mechanism — winners get re-released, studied in film schools, added to streaming front pages, and remembered as 'great films.' If the Best Picture choice no longer correlates with cultural memory, the Academy is losing a slice of soft power. By 2019, ratings for the broadcast had fallen from a 1998 peak of 55 million US viewers (Titanic year) to under 30 million. Coupled with debates around #OscarsSoWhite and the Best Popular Film proposal, the question of relevance is sharper than ever.

The list is a counter-history of Hollywood as remembered by audiences, not as honored by the Academy.

sentences.summary: det_07: Genre bias in IMDb connections. Source: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope (1977) - Connections (https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0076759/movieconnections) Facts: Star Wars has the most connections of any film in IMDb's frozen 2017 dataset (4965 in this set)

raw_evidence.label: Genre bias in IMDb connections
raw_evidence.content: Sci-fi, horror, action and comedy films are over-represented in connection counts because they generate quotable lines, iconic shots, and parody-friendly tropes. Star Wars (4965 references) and The Wizard of Oz (3291) lead the all-time list — neither won Best Picture. Psycho's shower scene, Jaws' two-note theme, and Terminator's 'I'll be back' are referenced thousands of times. By contrast, intimate dramas that win Best Picture — Spotlight, Moonlight, The Artist, Birdman — are rarely parodied or visually quoted. The dataset captures a specific kind of cultural memory: the kind that propagates through pastiche.

Source: README: 2019-03-02_oscars-influence (https://github.com/TheEconomist/graphic-detail-data/blob/master/data/2019-03-02_) Facts: annual_share = count / sum(count for films in same release_year); The top 100 per year are ranked from largest to smallest

raw_evidence.label: The recency problem
raw_evidence.content: A film from 1965 has had 50 extra years to accumulate references compared to a film from 2015. Connections counts therefore are not directly comparable across decades — they confound cultural impact with simple time elapsed. The Economist's solution was annual share: each film's count divided by the total references for all films released in the same year. Within any single year, share is a fair comparison; across years, it is still imperfect (older years are saturated and stable, the most recent years are still accruing). The chart deliberately ranks films within years rather than across years, but trends in the top-1 share or top-10 concentration over time can still be read.

raw_evidence.label: Concentration of references — share of #1 film, by decade
raw_evidence.content: The most-referenced film of each year used to dominate. In the 1970s the year-#1 captured 22.6% of all references on average. In the 2000s this fell to 7.2%, and in the 2010s to just 5.7% — a 4x drop. This is partly a function of the long tail of TV references and remake-saturation, but the underlying point is that any single film, including the Best Picture winner, has less cultural gravity in the streaming era than in the studio era. The maximum single-year share is Star Wars at 55.2% (1977); the 2010s peak is just 9.0%.

sentences.summary: det_06: Why this matters: the Oscars' cultural authority. Source: Statista: Academy Awards Viewership (https://www.statista.com/statistics/253743/academy-awards--number-of-viewers/) Facts: Oscars peaked at 55.25 million US viewers in 1998 (the Titanic year); Viewership fell to 26.5 million in 2018 | det_07: Genre bias in IMDb connections. Source: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope (1977) - Connections (https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0076759/movieconnections) Facts: Star Wars has the most connections of any film in IMDb's frozen 2017 dataset (4965 in this set)

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the Oscars' cultural authority
raw_evidence.content: The Academy Awards are the most-watched film awards in the world and have historically functioned as a canonization mechanism — winners get re-released, studied in film schools, added to streaming front pages, and remembered as 'great films.' If the Best Picture choice no longer correlates with cultural memory, the Academy is losing a slice of soft power. By 2019, ratings for the broadcast had fallen from a 1998 peak of 55 million US viewers (Titanic year) to under 30 million. Coupled with debates around #OscarsSoWhite and the Best Popular Film proposal, the question of relevance is sharper than ever.

sources.title: Statista: Academy Awards Viewership
facts: Oscars peaked at 55.25 million US viewers in 1998 (the Titanic year)
Viewership fell to 26.5 million in 2018

raw_evidence.label: Genre bias in IMDb connections
raw_evidence.content: Sci-fi, horror, action and comedy films are over-represented in connection counts because they generate quotable lines, iconic shots, and parody-friendly tropes. Star Wars (4965 references) and The Wizard of Oz (3291) lead the all-time list — neither won Best Picture. Psycho's shower scene, Jaws' two-note theme, and Terminator's 'I'll be back' are referenced thousands of times. By contrast, intimate dramas that win Best Picture — Spotlight, Moonlight, The Artist, Birdman — are rarely parodied or visually quoted. The dataset captures a specific kind of cultural memory: the kind that propagates through pastiche.
